questions.topic: Government as an Institution of the State
questions.stem: The body of persons and institutions that makes, enforces and interprets the laws of a state at any given time is the
questions.explanation: Government is the agency through which the state acts; it makes, executes and adjudicates laws, whereas the nation and electorate are not institutions of that kind.

questions.topic: Government as an Institution of the State
questions.stem: Which of the following distinguishes the state from the government?
options: The government has a defined territory but the state does not
The state is permanent while governments come and go
The state is made up only of elected officials
The government owns sovereignty while the state merely borrows it
Only the government has a population
questions.explanation: The state endures as a political community while the persons who form the government change through elections, coups or appointments.

questions.topic: Government as an Institution of the State
questions.stem: Kunle says that the "government of Ekiti State has decided to build a new hospital". In this statement, government is used to mean
options: an academic subject taught in schools
the activity of studying political theory
questions.explanation: Here government refers to the institution and persons who hold authority and take decisions on behalf of the state.

questions.topic: Government as a Process or Art of Governing
questions.stem: Government viewed as a process refers mainly to
options: the buildings and offices in which government ministries are housed
the list of subjects taught in political science
the total population of a country
the national boundaries of a state
the activities by which policies are made and carried out
questions.explanation: As a process, government is the continuous activity of ruling: formulating, implementing and reviewing policies.

questions.topic: Government as a Process or Art of Governing
questions.stem: Which of the following activities BEST illustrates government as an art of governing?
options: A student reading a textbook about the origin and nature of the state
A citizen paying a visit to a museum
A lecturer marking political science scripts
A governor negotiating with labour unions to end a strike
A trader keeping records of his sales
questions.explanation: The art of governing involves the skilful management of people and conflicts by those in authority, as when a governor negotiates to end a strike.

questions.topic: Government as a Process or Art of Governing
questions.stem: The process of government involves all the following EXCEPT
options: the formulation of policies by the executive
the enactment of laws by the legislature
the interpretation of laws by the courts
the implementation of decisions by the civil service
the private settlement of a debt between two traders
questions.explanation: A purely private transaction between two traders is not an act of ruling; the other options are stages in the governmental process.

questions.topic: Government as an Academic Field of Study
questions.stem: Ada tells her father that she studies Government in SS2. In that sense, Government refers to
options: the measurement of rainfall and climate
the systematic study of the state, its institutions and processes
the origin and spread of the major religions of the world over time
questions.explanation: Government as a discipline studies political institutions, processes, ideas and behaviour.

questions.topic: Government as an Academic Field of Study
questions.stem: One reason for studying Government in secondary schools is to
options: prepare citizens to understand their rights and duties
train students to become professional soldiers
qualify students automatically for elective office
replace the teaching of history and geography
enable students to avoid paying taxes and levies to the government
questions.explanation: The subject equips young people with knowledge of rights, duties and political institutions so that they can participate responsibly.

questions.topic: Government as an Academic Field of Study
questions.stem: Government as an academic discipline is closely related to all the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Government borrows from other social sciences and law; geometry is a branch of mathematics with no direct link to the study of political institutions.

questions.stem: The supreme and final legal authority of the state above which no further legal authority exists is called
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the supreme power of the state to make and enforce laws without being subject to any higher authority.

questions.stem: Power that is recognised as lawful and rightful by those over whom it is exercised is
questions.explanation: Authority is power that has been legitimised, so that people obey because they accept the right of the ruler to command.

questions.stem: Legitimacy is said to exist when
options: the government controls a large army
the leaders are wealthy and educated
the state has a written constitution only
the country belongs to many international bodies
the people accept the right of their rulers to govern
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is the acceptance by the governed that those in power have the right to rule.

questions.stem: A group of people bound together by common history, language and culture and who desire to live together is a
questions.explanation: A nation is a cultural community sharing a sense of common identity; a state is a political and legal entity with sovereignty.

questions.stem: Bisi lists the attributes that make Nigeria a state. Which item on her list is NOT an essential attribute of statehood?
questions.explanation: The United Kingdom is a state without a single written constitution; population, territory, government and sovereignty are the essential features.

questions.stem: A teacher persuades her students to join an environmental club without threats or rewards. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Influence is the ability to affect the behaviour of others through persuasion rather than through legal command or force.

questions.stem: The concept of political culture refers to
options: the traditional dances performed at political rallies
the number of political parties in a country
the distribution of power between levels of government
the formal rules contained in a written constitution and in the statutes of parliament
the attitudes, beliefs and values of a people towards their political system
questions.explanation: Political culture is the pattern of orientations people hold towards politics and the political system.

questions.stem: The process by which individuals acquire political values and attitudes through the family, school and peer groups is known as
questions.explanation: Political socialisation transmits political beliefs and values from one generation to another through agents such as family, school, media and peers.

questions.stem: The principle that no one is above the law and that all persons are equal before it is
questions.explanation: The rule of law, popularised by A. V. Dicey, stresses supremacy of the law, equality before the law and protection of rights.

questions.stem: The French writer whose book The Spirit of the Laws argued that liberty depends on dividing governmental power was
questions.explanation: Montesquieu argued in The Spirit of the Laws (1748) that liberty is safest when legislative, executive and judicial powers are held by separate bodies.

questions.stem: A President withholds assent from a bill and the National Assembly later overrides him by a two-thirds vote. This exchange illustrates
questions.explanation: The veto allows the executive to restrain the legislature, which can in turn override it by a two-thirds majority; this is checks and balances.

questions.stem: The power of the courts to declare an act of the legislature or executive null and void if it conflicts with the constitution is
questions.explanation: Judicial review enables the courts to strike down laws or actions that are inconsistent with the constitution.

questions.stem: Which of these constitutional arrangements weakens the idea that all persons are equally subject to the ordinary courts?
options: The existence of a written constitution
The immunity enjoyed by certain public officers while in office
questions.explanation: Constitutional immunity from civil and criminal proceedings for some officials while in office means they are not equally subject to the ordinary processes of the law.

questions.stem: Delegated legislation refers to
options: laws made by delegates at a party convention
bills sponsored jointly by two legislators
laws passed by a legislature and signed by the head of state after full public debate
laws made by bodies other than the legislature under authority given by the legislature
resolutions adopted by an international organisation
questions.explanation: Under delegated legislation, a parliament authorises ministers, local councils or agencies to make bye-laws, orders or regulations.

questions.stem: One major advantage of delegated legislation is that it
options: completely removes the need for a legislature
gives the judiciary power to make all laws
allows technical rules to be made quickly by experts
prevents the courts from reviewing any rule
ensures that every rule is debated in parliament
questions.explanation: Delegated legislation saves parliamentary time and lets experts make detailed technical regulations rapidly.

questions.stem: The principle of representative government is based on the idea that
options: every citizen must attend the legislature to vote on bills
people choose others to make decisions on their behalf
only the educated should take part in politics
the head of state appoints all legislators
political parties are unnecessary in a democracy
questions.explanation: In a representative government citizens elect representatives who make laws and policies on their behalf.

questions.stem: The document or body of rules that establishes the organs of a state and sets the limits of their powers is
options: a document listing the names of all citizens
the body of fundamental rules and principles by which a state is governed
the annual budget of a government
the manifesto of the ruling party
the code of conduct prescribed for civil servants and public officers only
questions.explanation: A constitution sets out the fundamental rules on how a state is organised, how power is distributed and the rights of citizens.

questions.stem: Britain has no single constitutional document. One of the places from which its constitutional rules are drawn is
questions.explanation: Conventions, together with statutes, common law, judicial precedents and authoritative works, are sources of the unwritten British constitution.

questions.stem: Customs and practices which are not written down as law but are observed in the running of government are called
questions.explanation: Conventions are unwritten rules of political practice that are binding by custom rather than by law.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT normally be a source of a constitution?
options: The private diary of a party member
questions.explanation: Constitutions draw on historical documents, statutes, judicial decisions, conventions and learned writings, not on private diaries.

questions.stem: A constituent assembly is a body set up mainly to
questions.explanation: A constituent assembly deliberates on and adopts a draft constitution, as Nigeria did in 1977-78 and 1988-89.

questions.stem: One major function of a constitution is to
options: fix the prices of goods in the market
define the powers and limits of the organs of government
choose the members of the cabinet
decide the result of every election
provide paid employment for all citizens who have completed their education
questions.explanation: A constitution establishes the organs of government and sets out the limits of their powers.

questions.stem: A constitution protects citizens against arbitrary government mainly by
options: increasing the number of police officers
making the head of state a life ruler
allowing the army to make laws
questions.explanation: Entrenched rights in a constitution limit what government may do to individuals and can be enforced in court.

questions.stem: A constitution performs many tasks. Which of the following lies OUTSIDE its proper role?
options: Defining the relationship between the governed and the government
Stating the procedure for its own amendment
Providing for the distribution of powers between levels of government
Serving as a reference point for settling constitutional disputes
Determining which party will win the next election
questions.explanation: A constitution sets the rules of the game but does not decide which party wins an election.

questions.stem: Where changing a constitution demands more than the ordinary law-making process, such as special majorities, the constitution is
questions.explanation: A rigid constitution can be changed only through a special procedure that is more difficult than ordinary law-making.

questions.stem: The constitution of the United Kingdom is best described as
questions.explanation: The British constitution is not contained in a single document and can be amended by an ordinary Act of Parliament.

questions.stem: The 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) is
questions.explanation: It is contained in a single document, has a special amendment procedure under section 9, and divides powers between federal and state governments.

questions.stem: One advantage of a flexible constitution is that it
options: gives absolute protection to minority rights
cannot be changed by any government
is always contained in one document
can easily be adapted to changing circumstances
requires a referendum for every amendment
questions.explanation: A flexible constitution can be amended by ordinary legislative procedure and so adapts readily to new situations.

questions.stem: A major disadvantage of a rigid constitution is that it
options: gives too much power to the courts
allows easy alteration of fundamental rights
may be too slow to respond to urgent needs of society
questions.explanation: Because amendment is difficult and time-consuming, a rigid constitution may fail to adapt quickly to changing social needs.

questions.stem: A proposed alteration to the 1999 Constitution (not one affecting state creation or fundamental rights) has passed both chambers of the National Assembly by two-thirds. Before it can proceed it must still be approved by the Houses of Assembly of
options: a simple majority of all the states
all the states of the Federation
not less than two-thirds of all the states
not less than one-half of the states and the Federal Capital Territory
not less than one-third of the states
questions.explanation: Section 9(2) requires a two-thirds vote in each House of the National Assembly and approval by resolution of the Houses of Assembly of not less than two-thirds of all the states.

questions.stem: A constitution under which the powers of government are concentrated in a single central authority is
questions.explanation: A unitary constitution vests all governmental power in a central government, which may delegate some functions to local units.

questions.stem: In a democracy, bills are debated, amended and passed by the
questions.explanation: The legislature debates and passes laws; in Nigeria at federal level this is the National Assembly.

questions.stem: A senator from Kano and a member representing a federal constituency in Enugu both belong to the National Assembly. The second person sits in the
questions.explanation: Section 47 of the 1999 Constitution establishes a bicameral National Assembly of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

questions.stem: The Nigerian Senate has a total membership of
questions.explanation: Each of the 36 states elects three senators and the FCT elects one, giving 109 senators.

questions.stem: The membership of the Nigerian House of Representatives is
questions.explanation: Section 49 provides for 360 members of the House of Representatives elected from federal constituencies.

questions.stem: A land dispute decided by the Court of Appeal can be taken on final appeal to the
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court is the final appellate court in Nigeria and is headed by the Chief Justice of Nigeria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the executive?
questions.explanation: The executive carries laws and policies into effect; interpretation belongs to the courts and impeachment and confirmation to the legislature.

questions.stem: After the National Judicial Council recommends a candidate and the President makes the nomination, the appointment of a new Chief Justice of Nigeria must be confirmed by the
questions.explanation: Section 231(1) provides that the CJN is appointed by the President on the recommendation of the NJC, subject to confirmation by the Senate.

questions.stem: The main reason for the bicameral legislature in a federation such as Nigeria is to
options: give equal representation to the federating units in one chamber
allow the President to dissolve one house whenever it rejects an executive bill
enable the judiciary to make laws
questions.explanation: In the Senate each state has equal representation (three senators), while the House of Representatives reflects population; this protects the interests of the federating units.

questions.stem: Independence of the judiciary in Nigeria is promoted by all the following EXCEPT
options: allowing the President to remove judges at will
charging judicial salaries on the Consolidated Revenue Fund
appointment of judges on the advice of the National Judicial Council
immunity of judges from actions for judicial acts
questions.explanation: Judges cannot be removed at the will of the President; removal follows constitutional procedure involving the NJC and, for senior judges, the legislature.

questions.stem: In Nigeria, a bill becomes law after it has been passed by the National Assembly and
options: approved by the Council of State
published by the Independent National Electoral Commission
questions.explanation: A bill passed by both Houses becomes law on receiving the President's assent, or if the National Assembly overrides a withheld assent by a two-thirds majority.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A system of government in which powers are shared between a central government and component units, each supreme in its own sphere, is
questions.explanation: In a federation the constitution divides power between the centre and the component units so that each is coordinate and independent within its sphere.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: In a confederation, the central government is
options: the only source of all legislation
questions.explanation: A confederation is a loose union in which the member states retain sovereignty and the centre exercises only limited delegated powers.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A feature of the parliamentary system of government is
options: a fixed term of office for the head of government
strict separation of personnel between organs
an executive president who is not a member of parliament
fusion of the executive and legislature
questions.explanation: In the parliamentary system ministers are drawn from and remain members of the legislature, so executive and legislature are fused.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: Under the parliamentary system, the government may be forced to resign if it
options: fails to win a court case brought against one of its ministers
refuses to attend a state banquet
loses a vote of no confidence in parliament
delays the publication of an annual report
questions.explanation: A government in a parliamentary system depends on the confidence of the legislature and must resign or call an election if it loses a vote of confidence.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: The presidential system of government is characterised by
options: collective responsibility of all ministers to the parliament that produced them
a single executive who is both head of state and head of government
a ceremonial head of state with no executive powers
a Prime Minister chosen from the majority party in parliament
the existence of a shadow cabinet
questions.explanation: In the presidential system one person, the President, is both head of state and head of government.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A system of government in which political power is held by a few wealthy people is
questions.explanation: Plutocracy is government by the rich.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A government based on religious authority and run by religious leaders is
questions.explanation: A theocracy is a state governed in the name of God or a religion, usually by religious leaders.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of a totalitarian state?
options: The state seeks to control every aspect of the lives of citizens
Opposition parties compete freely and openly in regular multiparty elections
The press is free to criticise the government
Power is divided between independent organs
The courts freely review executive actions
questions.explanation: Totalitarian regimes recognise no limits to state authority and aim to control political, economic, social and even private life.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A country in which the head of state is a hereditary monarch whose powers are limited by a constitution is a
questions.explanation: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch reigns but real power is exercised by elected officials within constitutional limits.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A state in which the head of state is elected or appointed and is not a hereditary monarch is a
questions.explanation: A republic has a head of state who holds office through election or appointment rather than by heredity.

questions.stem: A person who is a full member of a state and enjoys its rights and protection is a
questions.explanation: A citizen is a legal member of a state entitled to its rights and bound by its obligations.

questions.stem: Mr Hassan, a foreigner who has lived and worked in Nigeria for many years with good character, applies to become a Nigerian. The method open to him is
questions.explanation: Sections 25, 26 and 27 provide for citizenship by birth, registration and naturalisation respectively.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, a non-Nigerian woman who is or has been married to a citizen of Nigeria may become a citizen by
questions.explanation: Section 26(2)(a) allows a woman who is or has been married to a Nigerian citizen to be registered as a citizen.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, a Nigerian citizen may hold the citizenship of another country in addition, provided that the person is a citizen of Nigeria by
questions.explanation: Section 28 preserves dual citizenship only for citizens by birth; a registered or naturalised citizen forfeits Nigerian citizenship by acquiring another.

questions.stem: Of the following, which one is a duty that the citizen owes the state rather than a right he enjoys?
questions.explanation: Payment of taxes is a duty owed to the state; the other options are rights the citizen enjoys.

questions.stem: A person who lives in a country but is not a citizen of that country is called
questions.explanation: An alien is a person residing in a state of which he is not a citizen.

questions.stem: The renunciation of Nigerian citizenship is done by
options: the National Assembly passing a special resolution of both its chambers sitting jointly
a court ordering the citizen to leave the country
the Inspector-General of Police signing a warrant
a citizen of full age making a declaration in the prescribed manner
the citizen failing to vote in two elections
questions.explanation: Section 29 allows a citizen of full age who wishes to renounce Nigerian citizenship to make a declaration in the prescribed manner for registration.

questions.stem: The deprivation of citizenship under the 1999 Constitution applies to persons who became citizens by
questions.explanation: Section 30 empowers the President to deprive a registered or naturalised citizen of citizenship in specified circumstances; citizens by birth cannot be deprived.

questions.stem: An organised group of people with similar political ideas who seek to control government by winning elections is a
questions.explanation: The main aim of a political party, unlike a pressure group, is to capture and exercise governmental power.

questions.stem: The main difference between a political party and a pressure group is that a political party
options: does not have any membership register or organised branches anywhere
is not allowed to hold meetings
is financed only by foreign donors
seeks to win elections and form the government
questions.explanation: A pressure group seeks to influence policy without taking over government; a party contests elections to gain power.

questions.stem: When a party combines the demands of farmers, traders and students into a single programme, it is performing the function of
questions.explanation: Parties gather and combine various demands into policy programmes; registration of voters is done by the electoral body.

questions.stem: A party that is not in power and criticises the policies of the government is the
questions.explanation: The opposition checks the government by criticising policies and offering alternatives.

questions.stem: A document in which a political party sets out its programmes and promises to the electorate is the
questions.explanation: The manifesto states what the party intends to do if voted into office.

questions.stem: In Nigeria, the body constitutionally empowered to register political parties is the
questions.explanation: Under the 1999 Constitution and the Third Schedule, INEC registers and monitors political parties.

questions.stem: A political system in which only one party is legally permitted to exist is
questions.explanation: In a one-party system the constitution or law allows only one party to operate.

questions.stem: The United States of America is usually cited as an example of
questions.explanation: Although other parties exist, the Democratic and Republican parties dominate American politics.

questions.stem: Nigeria operates a
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution allows any association meeting the requirements to be registered, so many parties exist.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of the multi-party system is that it
options: may lead to unstable coalition governments
questions.explanation: With many parties, no single party may win a majority, leading to coalitions that can be unstable.

questions.stem: One advantage of the one-party system is that it
options: offers voters a wide choice of competing programmes and rival leaders
may promote national unity in a divided society
encourages strong opposition to the government
prevents the abuse of power completely
questions.explanation: Supporters argue that a single party can unite diverse groups, although it limits choice and may encourage dictatorship.

questions.stem: An organised group that seeks to influence government policy without seeking to form the government is a
questions.explanation: Pressure groups promote their members' interests by influencing decision-makers rather than contesting for power.

questions.stem: The Nigeria Labour Congress is an example of
questions.explanation: The NLC protects the interests of its members, the workers, so it is a sectional or interest group.

questions.stem: The practice of meeting legislators privately to persuade them to support a particular bill is known as
questions.explanation: Lobbying is a method by which pressure groups try to influence legislators and officials.

questions.stem: A spontaneous and unorganised group that emerges suddenly to protest and may resort to violence is
questions.explanation: Anomic groups arise spontaneously, often in riots or demonstrations, without formal organisation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a method used by pressure groups?
questions.explanation: Nominating candidates is a function of political parties, not of pressure groups.

questions.stem: A group that seeks to promote a cause of general public interest, such as protection of the environment, is called
questions.explanation: Promotional or cause groups pursue causes beneficial to society as a whole rather than the sectional interest of members.

questions.stem: The views held by a significant part of the population on issues of public concern is known as
questions.explanation: Public opinion is the aggregate of views held by a large section of the public on matters of common interest.

questions.stem: A research firm asks a sample of 2,000 adults what they think about a new tax. The firm is using
questions.explanation: Opinion polls, referendums, elections and media reports are used to gauge public opinion.

questions.stem: Public opinion is important in a democracy because it
options: makes regular elections unnecessary since leaders already know what the people want
replaces the work of the legislature
gives the military power to rule
guides government on the wishes of the people
questions.explanation: Public opinion informs government about the feelings of citizens so that policies reflect popular wishes.

questions.stem: Which of the following can distort public opinion?
questions.explanation: Propaganda presents one-sided or misleading information that shapes opinion artificially.

questions.stem: The mass media is often described as the
questions.explanation: The press is called the fourth estate because of its watchdog role alongside the three organs of government.

questions.stem: The regulatory body for radio and television broadcasting in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: The National Broadcasting Commission licenses and regulates broadcasting in Nigeria.

questions.stem: One function of the mass media in a democracy is to
options: conduct general elections and announce the official results on behalf of the commission
educate and inform the public on government activities
questions.explanation: The media informs and educates citizens and serves as a link between government and the governed.

questions.stem: A factor that limits the role of the mass media in Nigeria is
options: the high literacy rate of all citizens in both the urban and rural areas
government ownership and control of some media outlets
the existence of the Freedom of Information Act
the right to freedom of expression
the large number of private radio stations
questions.explanation: Government ownership can lead to bias and self-censorship, restricting the media's watchdog role.

questions.stem: The right to vote in elections is known as
questions.explanation: Franchise or suffrage is the right to vote.

questions.stem: In Nigeria, the minimum voting age is
questions.explanation: Section 77(2) and related provisions give every citizen who has attained 18 years and is registered the right to vote.

questions.stem: In a constituency, A scores 40%, B 35% and C 25% of the votes, and A is declared winner. The electoral system used is the
questions.explanation: Under first-past-the-post the candidate with most votes wins, regardless of whether he has over half of the votes.

questions.stem: A direct vote by the electorate on a specific issue of public importance is a
questions.explanation: A referendum allows voters to decide directly on a particular question such as a constitutional change.

questions.stem: A ruling party redraws ward boundaries so that its supporters form a majority in most of them. This practice is
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering manipulates boundaries for partisan advantage; delimitation is the neutral division of an area into constituencies.

questions.stem: Under section 134 of the 1999 Constitution, a candidate is duly elected President where there are two or more candidates if he has the highest number of votes and not less than one-quarter of the votes cast in at least
options: one-half of all the states and the Federal Capital Territory combined
two-thirds of all the states and the Federal Capital Territory
all the states of the Federation
questions.explanation: Section 134(2) requires the majority of votes plus at least 25% of the votes in each of at least two-thirds of the states and the FCT.

questions.stem: An election held to fill a vacancy that arises in a legislature between general elections is a
questions.explanation: A by-election fills a seat that becomes vacant through death, resignation or other causes.

questions.stem: Governorship and National Assembly elections in Nigeria are organised and supervised by the
questions.explanation: INEC organises, undertakes and supervises elections to federal and state offices.

questions.stem: In Nigeria, local government council elections are conducted by the
questions.explanation: Section 197 and the Third Schedule give State Independent Electoral Commissions power to conduct local government elections.

questions.stem: The device introduced by INEC to verify voters by fingerprint or facial recognition and to upload results is the
questions.explanation: The Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) authenticates voters biometrically and transmits polling unit results.

questions.stem: A losing candidate wants to challenge a governorship result. Which task would INEC itself NOT perform in this matter or generally?
options: Monitoring of the finances of political parties
questions.explanation: Election petitions are heard by election tribunals and courts, not by the electoral commission.

questions.stem: The electoral body which conducted the general elections that ushered in the Second Republic in 1979 was the
questions.explanation: FEDECO conducted the 1979 elections; NEC and NECON were bodies of later military transition programmes and INEC was set up in 1998.

questions.stem: Officials who remain in their posts whatever party wins an election and who carry out the policies of the government in power make up the
questions.explanation: The civil service is the body of permanent officials who implement government policy irrespective of the party in office.

questions.stem: Mrs Okafor, a director in a federal ministry, refuses to campaign for any party during an election. She is observing the civil service principle of
questions.explanation: Civil servants are expected to be politically neutral so that they can serve any government loyally.

questions.stem: The principle that civil servants should not be personally named or blamed in public for the policies they help to make is
questions.explanation: Under anonymity the minister, not the civil servant, takes public responsibility for the ministry's actions.

questions.stem: In a Nigerian federal ministry, the most senior career civil servant who serves as administrative head is the
options: Head of Service of the State
questions.explanation: The Permanent Secretary is the administrative head of a ministry and the minister's chief adviser.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common problem of the civil service in Nigeria?
options: Too much political neutrality among officers
A shortage of ministries to manage
Total absence of rules of conduct for staff
questions.explanation: Red tape, delay, corruption and over-staffing are frequently cited problems of the Nigerian public service.

questions.stem: The civil service reform of 1988 in Nigeria was significant because it
options: made the minister the chief executive and accounting officer of the ministry
transferred the civil service to state control
merged the civil service with the armed forces
questions.explanation: The 1988 reform made ministers chief executives and accounting officers of their ministries and professionalised the service, among other changes.

questions.stem: A major function of the civil service is to
options: pass laws for the federation and approve the annual appropriation bill
advise ministers and implement government policies
questions.explanation: Civil servants supply information and advice for policy-making and then carry the approved policies into effect.

questions.stem: The body responsible for appointing, promoting and disciplining federal civil servants in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: The Federal Civil Service Commission handles appointment, promotion and discipline in the federal civil service.

questions.stem: A state governor wants to fill vacancies in the state ministries with his campaign supporters. The existence of a Civil Service Commission is meant to
options: reduce the salaries of public servants
collect taxes on behalf of government
insulate appointments and discipline from political interference
questions.explanation: A Civil Service Commission ensures that recruitment and promotion follow merit rather than political patronage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of a Civil Service Commission?
options: Recruitment of staff into the civil service
Making laws for the conduct of elections
questions.explanation: Electoral laws are made by the legislature; the commission deals with personnel matters of the civil service.

questions.stem: A government-owned enterprise set up by law to provide essential services on a commercial basis is a
questions.explanation: A public corporation is a statutory body owned by government to provide services or goods, often on commercial lines.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a public corporation in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: The Nigerian Ports Authority is a statutory body owned by the federal government; the others are pressure groups.

questions.stem: Public corporations are controlled by the legislature mainly through
options: the appointment of their managing directors and other members of the board
the payment of their staff salaries
the conduct of their board meetings
the examination of their accounts and annual reports
questions.explanation: Parliamentary control is exercised through debates, committee probes and scrutiny of accounts and reports.

questions.stem: The sale of government shares in public enterprises to private investors is called
questions.explanation: Privatisation transfers ownership of public enterprises wholly or partly to private hands.

questions.stem: The policy under which government retains ownership of an enterprise but requires it to operate profitably without subsidies is known as
questions.explanation: Under commercialisation the enterprise remains public but must run on commercial principles and cover its costs.

questions.stem: One reason why public corporations in Nigeria often perform poorly is
options: the lack of any legal backing
the refusal of the courts to hear their cases
questions.explanation: Political appointments, interference and corruption have undermined efficiency in many public enterprises.

questions.stem: The level of government closest to the people at the grassroots is the
questions.explanation: Local government operates at the grassroots and provides services directly to communities.

questions.stem: The number of local government areas listed in the 1999 Constitution, including the area councils of the FCT, is
questions.explanation: The Constitution lists 768 local government areas in the states and 6 area councils in the FCT, a total of 774.

questions.stem: The local government reform which introduced a uniform, single-tier system of local government throughout Nigeria took place in
questions.explanation: The 1976 reform under the military government established a uniform, multi-purpose, single-tier local government system.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of local government under the Fourth Schedule of the 1999 Constitution?
options: Registration of births, deaths and marriages
Control and command of the armed forces of the Federation
questions.explanation: The Fourth Schedule assigns functions such as registration of births, deaths and marriages, markets and motor parks to local councils.

questions.stem: The account into which federal allocations to local governments in a state are paid before distribution is the
options: Consolidated Revenue Fund of the Federation
Treasury Single Account of the state
questions.explanation: Section 162(6) provides for a State Joint Local Government Account into which allocations to local councils in each state are paid.

questions.stem: In July 2024 the Supreme Court of Nigeria ruled that
options: state governors may dissolve elected local councils and appoint caretaker committees in their place
federal allocations due to local governments should be paid directly to them
local government elections should be conducted by INEC
local governments are agencies of the state ministry
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court held that allocations from the Federation Account belong to local governments and should be paid directly to them, and that dissolving democratically elected councils is unconstitutional.

questions.stem: A major problem confronting local governments in Nigeria is
options: too much revenue from internally generated sources
direct control by the United Nations
questions.explanation: State interference, inadequate funds and corruption hinder local government performance.

questions.stem: In the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani political system, the chief judge who administered Islamic law was the
questions.explanation: The Alkali presided over Sharia courts in the emirates.

questions.stem: In the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani emirate, the Waziri was the
options: commander of the army in all its wars against neighbouring states
chief adviser and head of administration
officer in charge of the capital city
questions.explanation: The Waziri was the most senior official, comparable to a prime minister, who advised the Emir.

questions.stem: The traditional title of the commander of the army in the old Oyo Empire was
questions.explanation: The Are-Ona-Kakanfo was the field commander of the Oyo army.

questions.stem: In the old Oyo Empire, the council of kingmakers headed by the Bashorun was the
questions.explanation: The Oyo Mesi chose the Alaafin and could reject him; it was led by the Bashorun.

questions.stem: In the old Oyo Empire, the body that served as a check on the power of the Oyo Mesi was the
questions.explanation: The Ogboni, a powerful cult of earth, mediated between the Alaafin and the Oyo Mesi and could check the latter.

questions.stem: The pre-colonial Igbo political system is often described as
questions.explanation: Most Igbo communities had no single central ruler; authority was diffused among elders, age grades and title holders.

questions.stem: In the traditional Igbo political system, the staff held by the eldest man of a lineage as a symbol of authority was the
questions.explanation: The Ofo staff symbolised ancestral authority, truth and justice and was held by the lineage head (Okpara).

questions.stem: Comparing an Igbo village-group with a Hausa-Fulani emirate before colonial rule, a student would rightly note that
options: the Igbo had a strong central monarch who ruled all of Igboland from one capital
the Hausa-Fulani had no system of taxation
authority was diffused among many bodies in the Igbo system
the Igbo used Sharia law in their courts
the Hausa-Fulani had no administrative officials
questions.explanation: The Hausa-Fulani emirates were centralised under the Emir, whereas Igbo society was largely segmentary and decentralised.

questions.stem: In the pre-colonial Benin Kingdom, the senior chiefs who acted as kingmakers were the
questions.explanation: The Uzama were hereditary chiefs who installed the Oba of Benin.

questions.stem: Which of the following taxes was levied on cattle in the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani emirates?
questions.explanation: Jangali was a cattle tax paid by herders; Kharaj was a land tax and Zakat a religious levy.

questions.stem: When the British governed Kano through its Emir, his officials and his courts, they were applying the policy of
questions.explanation: Indirect rule used existing traditional authorities to administer the people under British supervision.

questions.stem: The colonial administrator most associated with the introduction of indirect rule in Northern Nigeria was
questions.explanation: Lord Lugard introduced indirect rule in Northern Nigeria and wrote The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa.

questions.stem: Indirect rule was most successful in Northern Nigeria because
options: the people there were already literate in English
the British had abundant European manpower available to post to every district
there was an existing centralised system with taxes
the region had no traditional rulers
questions.explanation: The emirate system already had a hierarchy, courts and taxation which the British could easily use.

questions.stem: In Eastern Nigeria, the British appointed chiefs to administer communities that had no kings. These chiefs were known as
questions.explanation: Because most Igbo communities lacked kings, the British issued warrants to appointed chiefs, who were often resented.

questions.stem: In 1929 thousands of women in Owerri and Calabar provinces rose in protest; the Aba Women's Riot was directed chiefly at
options: the introduction of Western education and Christian schools in the villages
rumoured taxation of women and abusive warrant chiefs
the amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria
the ban on the slave trade
questions.explanation: Fears that women would be taxed and resentment of corrupt warrant chiefs sparked the 1929 women's protest.

questions.stem: Under the British colonial system, the official in charge of a province was the
questions.explanation: A Resident headed a province and supervised the native authorities through District Officers.

questions.stem: The French colonial policy which aimed at turning Africans into Frenchmen was
questions.explanation: Assimilation sought to make Africans culturally and politically French.

questions.stem: The four communes of Senegal whose inhabitants enjoyed French citizenship were Dakar, Goree, Rufisque and
questions.explanation: Inhabitants of the Four Communes, including Saint-Louis, could elect a deputy to the French parliament.

questions.stem: The French policy of association differed from assimilation in that it
options: granted all Africans French citizenship and equal political rights at once
abolished the use of chiefs entirely
made Africans members of the French parliament
allowed Africans to retain their culture under French control
questions.explanation: Association acknowledged differences between French and African cultures and dropped the goal of full assimilation.

questions.stem: The system of summary justice under which French administrators could punish Africans without trial was the
questions.explanation: The indigénat allowed administrators to impose penalties on African subjects without formal trial.

questions.stem: A major difference between British and French colonial administration was that the French
options: relied heavily on powerful traditional rulers to govern on their behalf in every colony
encouraged the development of local languages
did not tax their colonial subjects
practised no form of forced labour
used chiefs as mere agents of the central administration
questions.explanation: French chiefs were reduced to subordinate administrative agents, unlike the British who preserved traditional authority under indirect rule.

questions.stem: A historian assessing British rule in Nigeria lists both gains and losses. Which item belongs on the list of gains?
options: Erosion of the authority of traditional rulers
questions.explanation: Western education, though limited in reach, was an important legacy of colonial rule.

questions.stem: One negative economic effect of colonial rule on West Africa was
options: a balanced development of all regions, both coastal and in the interior
dependence on the export of raw materials
questions.explanation: Colonial economies were geared to producing cash crops and minerals for export, creating dependency on primary products.

questions.stem: The person often called the father of Nigerian nationalism is
questions.explanation: Herbert Macaulay founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in 1923 and is regarded as the father of Nigerian nationalism.

questions.stem: The first political party in Nigeria, the Nigerian National Democratic Party, was formed in
questions.explanation: Herbert Macaulay formed the NNDP in 1923 to contest the elective seats created by the Clifford Constitution.

questions.stem: The newspaper established by Nnamdi Azikiwe in 1937 which promoted nationalism was the
questions.explanation: The West African Pilot was a powerful nationalist paper founded by Azikiwe.

questions.stem: Northern members walked out of the House of Representatives in 1953 after an Action Group member proposed independence in 1956. The mover of that motion was
questions.explanation: Chief Anthony Enahoro of the Action Group moved the 1953 self-government motion, which led to a crisis and the Kano riots.

questions.stem: Which of the following stimulated the growth of nationalism in Nigeria after 1945?
options: The abolition of Western education in all mission schools across the colony
The introduction of indirect rule in 1900
The arrival of the Portuguese traders
The completion of the Lagos-Kano railway line
The return of ex-servicemen from the Second World War
questions.explanation: Ex-servicemen exposed to the world during the war and the Atlantic Charter fuelled demands for self-rule after 1945.

questions.stem: The West African Students' Union, which promoted nationalism among West Africans in Britain, was founded in 1925 by
questions.explanation: Ladipo Solanke founded WASU in London in 1925.

questions.stem: Under the Clifford Constitution of 1922, the right to vote in Lagos and Calabar was restricted to adult males who
options: were members of the Legislative Council
had served in the colonial army
earned an annual income of at least 100 pounds
questions.explanation: The franchise under the 1922 constitution was limited to adult male residents with a gross annual income of not less than 100 pounds.

questions.stem: A major weakness of the 1922 Clifford Constitution was that its Legislative Council
options: did not legislate for the Northern Provinces
had no official members at all
was made up only of Nigerians
was elected by universal adult suffrage
had power to remove the Governor
questions.explanation: The Legislative Council legislated only for the Colony and Southern Provinces; the North was governed by the Governor's proclamations.

questions.stem: Regionalism was first introduced into Nigeria by the
questions.explanation: The Richards Constitution created three regions (North, West and East), each with a regional House of Assembly.

questions.stem: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 differed from the Richards Constitution in that it
options: abolished the regions completely and restored a single central legislature
was drawn up after wide consultation with Nigerians
gave women universal suffrage throughout Nigeria
questions.explanation: Nationalists had criticised Richards for imposing a constitution; Macpherson consulted Nigerians at village, provincial, regional and national levels.

questions.stem: Which of the following was introduced by the Lyttelton Constitution of 1954?
options: A federal structure with regional premiers and separate regional public services
A unitary system of government with a single civil service
An executive President elected nationwide for a fixed term of five years
A two-party system decreed by the government
The abolition of the House of Chiefs in the North
questions.explanation: The 1954 constitution established a true federation: Lagos became federal territory, regions had premiers and their own public services and judiciaries.

questions.stem: The Willink Commission of 1957-58 was set up to
options: investigate the causes of the Kano riots of 1953 and recommend punishment
examine the fears of minorities and ways of allaying them
questions.explanation: The Willink Commission inquired into minority fears; it recommended entrenching fundamental rights rather than creating new states.

questions.stem: Under the 1946 constitution, the North alone had a bicameral regional legislature because it had a
options: Senate in addition to a House of Representatives
House of Chiefs in addition to a House of Assembly
Council of Ministers in addition to a Legislative Council
Privy Council in addition to an Executive Council
Native Court in addition to a Customary Court
questions.explanation: The Northern Region had both a House of Assembly and a House of Chiefs under the Richards Constitution.

questions.stem: Under the 1960 Independence Constitution, the ceremonial head of state representing the British monarch was the
questions.explanation: Nigeria remained a monarchy within the Commonwealth until 1963, with the Governor-General representing the Queen.

questions.stem: The 1963 Republican Constitution is significant because it
options: introduced the executive presidential system with a Vice-President
replaced the Governor-General with a ceremonial President
established the National Assembly with 109 senators
questions.explanation: The 1963 constitution made Nigeria a republic; a ceremonial President, Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe, replaced the British monarch as head of state.

questions.stem: The 1979 Constitution was drafted by a committee of forty-nine members chaired by
questions.explanation: The Constitution Drafting Committee of 1975-76 was chaired by Chief Rotimi Williams.

questions.stem: The principle of federal character first appeared in a Nigerian constitution in
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution introduced the requirement that appointments reflect the federal character of Nigeria.

questions.stem: The 1989 Constitution was unusual in that it
options: was approved by a national referendum held in all the states
provided for only two political parties
questions.explanation: The 1989 Constitution and the transition programme limited party politics to two government-created parties, the SDP and the NRC.

questions.stem: The 1999 Constitution of Nigeria was brought into force by
options: a referendum of all registered voters
a decree of the military government
an Act of the British Parliament
a resolution of the Constituent Assembly
a ruling of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: It was promulgated by the Abubakar military government through Decree No. 24 of 1999 and came into force on 29 May 1999.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The Nigerian political party formed in 1951 from the Yoruba cultural organisation Egbe Omo Oduduwa was the
options: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons
questions.explanation: The Action Group grew out of the Egbe Omo Oduduwa and was led by Chief Obafemi Awolowo.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The Northern People's Congress developed from a cultural association known as
questions.explanation: The NPC emerged from Jam'iyyar Mutanen Arewa, a northern cultural association, and became a party in 1951.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: A political party of the First Republic that drew its main support from the talakawa (commoners) of the North was the
questions.explanation: NEPU, led by Mallam Aminu Kano, championed the cause of the talakawa against the emirate establishment.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: Which of the following parties contested the 1979 general elections?
questions.explanation: The UPN, NPN, NPP, GNPP and PRP contested in 1979; the SDP was a party of the aborted Third Republic and the PDP and APC belong to the Fourth Republic.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The two political parties established by the military government for the aborted Third Republic were the
questions.explanation: The Babangida administration created the Social Democratic Party and the National Republican Convention in 1989.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: A common feature of the major political parties of the First Republic was that each
options: was founded by the colonial government
was banned by the colonial government shortly before the 1959 elections
had its main base in one region and among one major ethnic group
questions.explanation: The NPC, AG and NCNC were largely regional and ethnically based, which heightened tension in the First Republic.

questions.stem: The decrees made by a military government at the federal level were usually passed by its
options: Supreme Military Council or equivalent ruling council
questions.explanation: Under military rule the ruling council, such as the Supreme Military Council or the Provisional Ruling Council, exercised legislative powers.

questions.stem: Laws made by military governors for their states were known as
questions.explanation: The federal military government issued decrees while state military governors issued edicts.

questions.stem: Nigeria's Fourth Republic began on 29 May 1999 when the military government headed by
options: Murtala Mohammed handed over to a civilian government
Abdulsalami Abubakar handed over power to an elected civilian government
Yakubu Gowon handed over power to an elected President
Ibrahim Babangida handed over to the Interim National Government
Aguiyi-Ironsi handed over to the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: General Abdulsalami Abubakar completed a transition programme and handed over to an elected government on 29 May 1999.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a negative effect of military rule in Nigeria?
options: Creation of more states and the building of new roads and bridges
Establishment of the National Youth Service Corps
Suspension of parts of the constitution and of the legislature
Building of the new Federal Capital Territory
questions.explanation: Military regimes suspended constitutional provisions and dissolved legislatures, eroding democratic institutions.

questions.stem: The Interim National Government set up in August 1993 was headed by
questions.explanation: Chief Ernest Shonekan headed the Interim National Government until it was removed in November 1993.

questions.stem: The military government that handed over power to the civilian administration of the Second Republic in 1979 was headed by
questions.explanation: General Obasanjo, who succeeded Murtala Mohammed in 1976, handed over to an elected President on 1 October 1979.

questions.stem: Under military rule, the constitution was usually
questions.explanation: Military regimes suspended or modified constitutional provisions by decree.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: In Nigeria, the power to make laws on defence and foreign affairs belongs to the
options: National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly jointly
questions.explanation: Defence and external affairs are on the Exclusive Legislative List, on which only the National Assembly can legislate.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: A State House of Assembly wishes to pass a law. On which of these matters may it legislate alongside the National Assembly?
options: Immigration into and emigration from Nigeria
questions.explanation: Education beyond the primary level is on the Concurrent List; the other items are exclusive to the federal government.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: In the event of conflict between a valid federal law and a state law on a concurrent matter, the
options: state law prevails because the state government is closer to the people
federal law prevails and the state law is void to the extent of the inconsistency
matter is settled by a referendum in that state
Council of State decides which law applies
questions.explanation: Section 4(5) provides that a federal law prevails and the inconsistent state law is void to the extent of inconsistency.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: The body responsible for monitoring revenue accruals and recommending revenue allocation formulas in Nigeria is the
options: Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission
questions.explanation: The RMAFC monitors accruals into the Federation Account and reviews revenue allocation formulas.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: The 1999 Constitution provides that not less than what percentage of revenue from natural resources must be allocated on the principle of derivation?
questions.explanation: The proviso to section 162(2) requires that not less than 13% of revenue from natural resources be returned on the basis of derivation.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: Which of the following is a problem of Nigerian federalism?
options: The existence of a written constitution
The use of English as an official language
The membership of Nigeria in the United Nations
questions.explanation: Revenue allocation, census disputes, minority agitation and resource control remain contentious in Nigerian federalism.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: The Federal Character Commission was established to
options: conduct the national population and housing census every ten years
ensure fair distribution of public posts among the states
questions.explanation: The Commission enforces the federal character principle in appointments and the sharing of amenities.

questions.stem: The principles and objectives that guide a country in its relations with other countries are known as its
questions.explanation: Foreign policy is the set of goals and strategies a state pursues in its relations with other states.

questions.stem: Nigeria's leading role in the liberation of Southern African countries from minority rule showed its commitment to
options: the policy of non-alignment with the West only
the eradication of colonialism and racism in Africa
the promotion of military rule and one-party states across the continent of Africa
the expansion of trade with Europe
the protection of foreign oil companies
questions.explanation: Nigeria was regarded as a front-line state in the struggle against apartheid and minority rule.

questions.stem: The Nigerian scheme under which young professionals are sent to serve in other African, Caribbean and Pacific countries is the
questions.explanation: The Technical Aid Corps, set up in 1987, sends Nigerian professionals to serve in developing countries.

questions.stem: The concept of "concentric circles" in Nigeria's foreign policy places at the innermost circle
options: relations with the Western powers and their military alliances
the United Nations and its agencies
Nigeria's immediate neighbours and West African security
questions.explanation: The concentric circles approach gave priority first to Nigeria's neighbours, then West Africa, then Africa and finally the wider world.

questions.stem: The United Nations has its headquarters in
questions.explanation: The UN headquarters is in New York, United States.

questions.stem: How many permanent members does the United Nations Security Council have?
questions.explanation: The Security Council has 15 members, five of which (China, France, Russia, the UK and the USA) are permanent with veto power.

questions.stem: The headquarters of the African Union is located in
questions.explanation: The AU, like its predecessor the OAU, is headquartered in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

questions.stem: Nigeria became a member of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in
questions.explanation: Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971.

questions.stem: Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in 1995 mainly because of
options: its refusal to pay its dues to the United Nations and the African Union
the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and other Ogoni activists
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth suspended Nigeria in November 1995 after the execution of the Ogoni Nine; it was fully restored in 1999.

questions.stem: As of 2026, which of these West African countries still belongs to ECOWAS?
questions.explanation: Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso left ECOWAS with effect from January 2025; Chad belongs to Central Africa and is not an ECOWAS member; Senegal remains a member.

questions.topic: Government as an Institution of the State
questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between the state and the government. [5 marks]
(b) Explain five functions performed by government in a modern state. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: State is a politically organised community with territory, population, government and sovereignty
1 mark: Government is the agency/machinery through which the will of the state is expressed and carried out
1 mark: State is permanent; government changes (elections, coups)
1 mark: State is abstract; government is concrete, made up of identifiable persons
1 mark: Sovereignty belongs to the state; government only exercises it on behalf of the state
2 marks: Maintenance of law and order/internal security
2 marks: Defence of territorial integrity against external aggression
2 marks: Provision of social services and infrastructure (schools, hospitals, roads)
2 marks: Protection of the rights and liberties of citizens
2 marks: Management of the economy/conduct of foreign relations (any other valid function)
questions.explanation: The state is the enduring political community possessing population, defined territory, government and sovereignty; government is the institution through which the state acts. The state is permanent and abstract while governments are temporary and made up of identifiable officials who exercise sovereignty on behalf of the state. Functions of government include maintaining law and order through the police and courts, defending the country, providing social amenities such as schools and hospitals, protecting fundamental rights, regulating the economy and conducting external relations.

questions.stem:
(a) What is sovereignty? [3 marks]
(b) Explain four limitations on the sovereignty of a state such as Nigeria. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Sovereignty: the supreme, absolute and final legal power of the state to make and enforce laws within its territory without external control
3 marks: Constitutional limits, e.g. entrenched fundamental rights and separation of powers
3 marks: International law, treaties and membership of organisations such as the UN, AU and ECOWAS
3 marks: Public opinion, pressure groups and the threat of elections or revolt
3 marks: Economic dependence/foreign debt and conditions of donors, or customs and religion (any valid fourth limit)
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the supreme and final authority of the state to make and enforce laws over all persons and things within its territory, free from external control. In practice it is limited by the constitution (rights and the division of powers), by international law and treaty obligations such as ECOWAS protocols and UN resolutions, by public opinion and organised groups, and by economic dependence on creditors and trading partners, as well as by entrenched customs and religious beliefs.

questions.stem:
(a) Define delegated legislation. [3 marks]
(b) Give three forms of delegated legislation. [3 marks]
(c) Explain three ways by which delegated legislation is controlled. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Laws/rules made by bodies or persons other than the legislature under powers conferred on them by an enabling Act of the legislature
1 mark: Bye-laws of local government councils
1 mark: Statutory orders, rules and regulations made by ministers
1 mark: Orders-in-council/proclamations or rules of court and public corporations
3 marks: Legislative control: the enabling Act sets limits; rules may be laid before the legislature, which can amend or annul them
3 marks: Judicial control: courts may declare rules ultra vires and void if they exceed the enabling Act or the constitution
3 marks: Executive/administrative control or public opinion: ministers review rules, and the press and pressure groups expose abuses
questions.explanation: Delegated legislation consists of rules made by ministers, local councils, agencies and other bodies under authority granted by the legislature through an enabling law. Forms include bye-laws, statutory instruments and regulations, orders and rules of court. It is controlled by the legislature (through the terms of the parent Act, laying and annulment procedures and committee scrutiny), by the courts through the ultra vires doctrine, and by the executive, the press and public opinion.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five functions of a constitution. [10 marks]
(b) Identify five sources of a constitution. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Establishes the organs of government and defines their powers
2 marks: Limits the powers of government and prevents arbitrary rule
2 marks: Defines the relationship between the government and the governed; protects fundamental rights
2 marks: Provides for the distribution of powers between levels of government
2 marks: States the procedure for its own amendment/serves as reference for settling disputes
1 mark: Statutes/Acts of parliament
1 mark: Judicial precedents
1 mark: Conventions
1 mark: Historical documents and constitutional conferences
1 mark: Works of eminent writers/customs
questions.explanation: A constitution sets up the legislature, executive and judiciary and spells out their powers; it limits government and protects citizens' rights; it divides power among levels of government in a federation; and it provides the procedure for amendment and the yardstick for resolving constitutional disputes. Its sources include statutes, judicial decisions, conventions, historical documents and conferences, and learned authorities and customs.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain three ways by which a person may become a citizen of Nigeria under the 1999 Constitution. [9 marks]
(b) State three duties of a Nigerian citizen. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: By birth: born in or outside Nigeria to a parent or grandparent who is or was a Nigerian citizen (section 25)
3 marks: By registration: e.g. a woman married to a Nigerian man, or a person of full age born abroad whose grandparent was Nigerian (section 26)
3 marks: By naturalisation: an alien of full age and good character who has resided in Nigeria for the required period and satisfies other conditions (section 27)
2 marks: Obey the laws and respect constituted authority
2 marks: Pay taxes and rates promptly
2 marks: Defend the country/vote at elections/protect public property (any valid duty)
questions.explanation: Under Chapter III of the 1999 Constitution citizenship may be acquired by birth, by registration and by naturalisation. A citizen by birth has a Nigerian parent or grandparent; registration is open to, among others, foreign women married to Nigerian men; naturalisation is for aliens of full age and good character who have lived in Nigeria for a long period, are acceptable to the local community and take the oath of allegiance. Duties include obedience to law, payment of taxes, defence of the nation, voting and protecting public property.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a multi-party system? [3 marks]
(b) Give four advantages and two disadvantages of the multi-party system. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: A party system in which more than two parties compete for power and any of them may win or form a coalition
2 marks: Offers voters a wide choice of programmes and candidates
2 marks: Allows diverse interests and minorities to be represented
2 marks: Encourages effective opposition and accountability
2 marks: Promotes freedom of association and democracy
2 marks: May lead to unstable coalition governments
2 marks: May encourage ethnic/religious parties and political fragmentation
questions.explanation: A multi-party system is one in which several parties legally exist and compete for power. It widens voter choice, represents varied interests, strengthens opposition and accountability and reflects freedom of association. On the other hand it can produce weak or unstable coalitions, fragment the electorate along ethnic or religious lines, and make elections costly and confusing.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five roles of the mass media in a democracy. [10 marks]
(b) State five factors that limit the effectiveness of the mass media in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Informs and educates the public on government policies and events
2 marks: Serves as a watchdog, exposing corruption and abuse of power
2 marks: Provides a forum for public opinion and debate
2 marks: Links government and the governed/feedback channel
2 marks: Aids political socialisation and voter education
1 mark: Government ownership and control
1 mark: Harassment of journalists and restrictive laws
1 mark: Poor funding, power supply and equipment
1 mark: Bias, sensationalism and corruption of some journalists
1 mark: Illiteracy and poverty limiting access/spread of false information online
questions.explanation: The media inform and educate citizens, act as watchdogs over those in power, provide platforms for debate and the expression of public opinion, link rulers and ruled and teach political values. Their effectiveness is reduced by government ownership, intimidation and restrictive laws, inadequate funding and infrastructure, partisanship and unethical conduct, illiteracy and poverty among audiences, and the spread of misinformation on social media.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the proportional representation system of election. [4 marks]
(b) Give three advantages and two disadvantages of proportional representation. [10 marks]
(c) Name one country that uses a form of proportional representation. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Seats in the legislature are allocated to parties in proportion to the votes they receive, e.g. by party list or single transferable vote
2 marks: Fair representation of parties in proportion to their support
2 marks: Minorities and small parties gain representation
2 marks: Fewer wasted votes; encourages participation
2 marks: Often produces coalition and unstable governments
2 marks: Weak link between representatives and constituencies/complex to operate
1 mark: Any correct example, e.g. South Africa, Israel, the Netherlands
questions.explanation: Under proportional representation each party obtains a share of seats that matches its share of the vote, through list systems or the single transferable vote. It is fairer to small parties and minorities and wastes fewer votes, but it often leads to coalition governments, weakens the bond between legislators and constituencies and can be complex. South Africa, Israel and the Netherlands use forms of it.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five conditions necessary for the conduct of free and fair elections. [10 marks]
(b) State five electoral malpractices common in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: An independent and impartial electoral management body
2 marks: Universal adult suffrage and an accurate voters register
2 marks: Secret ballot
2 marks: Independent judiciary to settle election disputes
2 marks: Freedom of campaign, free press and neutral security agencies
1 mark: Vote buying
1 mark: Ballot snatching or stuffing
1 mark: Falsification of results
1 mark: Intimidation and violence against voters
1 mark: Under-age or multiple voting
questions.explanation: Free and fair elections require an independent electoral body, a credible register based on universal adult suffrage, secret voting, impartial security agencies, freedom of campaign and expression, and courts able to resolve disputes. Common malpractices include vote buying, ballot snatching and stuffing, falsification of results, voter intimidation and violence, and multiple or under-age voting.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five features of the civil service. [10 marks]
(b) Give five problems of the civil service in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Permanence: civil servants remain in office irrespective of changes of government
2 marks: Neutrality: they do not take part in partisan politics
2 marks: Anonymity: they are not publicly credited or blamed for policies
2 marks: Hierarchy: organised in grades with a clear chain of command
2 marks: Expertise and recruitment on merit/impartiality
1 mark: Corruption
1 mark: Red tape and delays
1 mark: Political interference
1 mark: Poor remuneration and low morale
1 mark: Over-staffing/ghost workers or nepotism in recruitment
questions.explanation: The civil service is permanent, politically neutral, anonymous, hierarchical and professional, recruiting on merit and serving any government impartially. In Nigeria it suffers from corruption, bureaucratic delays, political interference, poor pay and morale, over-staffing and ghost workers, and nepotism in recruitment and promotion.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four functions of the Federal Civil Service Commission in Nigeria. [8 marks]
(b) Explain how the independence of a Civil Service Commission may be guaranteed. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Appointment of persons into the federal civil service
2 marks: Promotion of civil servants
2 marks: Discipline, including dismissal, of erring officers
2 marks: Advising government on personnel policy/conducting examinations
2 marks: Members enjoy security of tenure and can be removed only for stated reasons
2 marks: Salaries charged on the Consolidated Revenue Fund
2 marks: Members appointed on merit and not subject to direction of any authority in their functions
1 mark: Members barred from partisan political activity
questions.explanation: The Federal Civil Service Commission appoints, promotes and disciplines federal civil servants and advises government on personnel matters. Its independence is protected when its members have security of tenure, their pay is charged on the Consolidated Revenue Fund, they are not subject to political direction in exercising their functions, and they are appointed on merit and kept out of partisan politics.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five features of the 1976 Local Government Reform in Nigeria. [10 marks]
(b) State five sources of revenue for local governments in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Introduced a uniform, single-tier local government system across the country
2 marks: Local government recognised as a third tier of government
2 marks: Statutory allocation of federal and state revenue to local councils
