2 marks: Elected councillors with a chairman as head
2 marks: Population criteria (about 150,000 to 800,000) and defined functions for councils; traditional rulers given advisory roles
1 mark: Statutory allocation from the Federation Account
1 mark: Share of state revenue
1 mark: Rates and levies
1 mark: Market and motor park fees
1 mark: Licences, fines and loans/grants
questions.explanation: The 1976 reform created a uniform single-tier system, made local government the third tier of government, guaranteed councils a share of federal and state revenue, provided for elected councillors and chairmen, laid down population guidelines and functions and gave traditional rulers advisory roles. Councils earn revenue from Federation Account allocations, state allocations, rates, market and motor park fees, licences, fines, grants and loans.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the political organisation of the pre-colonial Igbo society. [9 marks]
(b) Explain three reasons why indirect rule failed in Igboland. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Acephalous/segmentary: no central ruler; the village or village-group was the highest political unit
2 marks: Council of elders (Ama-ala) headed by the Okpara holding the Ofo made decisions
2 marks: Age grades performed executive functions such as public works and security
2 marks: Ozo and other title holders, oracles and diviners (e.g. Ibini Ukpabi) settled disputes
1 mark: Village assembly gave adult males a say: direct democracy
2 marks: Absence of traditional chiefs, so the British imposed unpopular warrant chiefs
2 marks: Warrant chiefs were corrupt and oppressive and lacked legitimacy
2 marks: Introduction of direct taxation and resistance such as the 1929 Aba women's protest
questions.explanation: Igbo society was decentralised. The village assembly of adult males deliberated on issues; councils of elders led by the Okpara, holder of the Ofo staff, made decisions; age grades executed them; Ozo titled men enjoyed influence; and oracles, dibia and secret societies served judicial and religious functions. Indirect rule failed because there were no chiefs to use, the warrant chiefs created by the British were illegitimate and corrupt, and the extension of direct taxation provoked resistance such as the 1929 women's protest.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five positive effects of colonial rule on Nigeria. [10 marks]
(b) Give five negative effects of colonial rule on Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Introduction of Western education
2 marks: Development of transport and communication infrastructure (railways, roads, ports)
2 marks: Unification of diverse peoples into one political entity
2 marks: Introduction of Western-type legal, administrative and parliamentary institutions
2 marks: Improved health services and abolition of inhuman practices
1 mark: Economic exploitation and dependence on cash crops
1 mark: Erosion of traditional authority and culture
1 mark: Uneven development between regions
1 mark: Ethnic rivalry fostered by divide-and-rule
1 mark: Neglect of industrialisation
questions.explanation: Colonial rule introduced Western education, built railways, roads and ports, brought diverse peoples into one state, created modern legal and administrative systems, and improved health care while ending some harmful practices. Negatively, it exploited resources, tied the economy to primary exports, undermined traditional institutions and culture, developed regions unevenly, encouraged ethnic rivalry and neglected industrial development.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five factors that contributed to the growth of nationalism in Nigeria. [10 marks]
(b) Mention five Nigerian nationalist leaders. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Western education, which produced an educated elite aware of rights
2 marks: Racial discrimination in appointments and social life
2 marks: Economic exploitation by colonial firms and government
2 marks: Effects of the Second World War, ex-servicemen and the Atlantic Charter
2 marks: Role of the press and independence of India/Ghana
1 mark: Herbert Macaulay
1 mark: Nnamdi Azikiwe
1 mark: Obafemi Awolowo
1 mark: Ahmadu Bello
1 mark: Anthony Enahoro/Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti/Aminu Kano/Tafawa Balewa (any)
questions.explanation: Nationalism grew from Western education, discrimination against educated Africans, economic exploitation, the experience of the Second World War and the Atlantic Charter, the nationalist press, and the example of India (1947) and Ghana (1957). Leaders include Herbert Macaulay, Nnamdi Azikiwe, Obafemi Awolowo, Ahmadu Bello, Anthony Enahoro, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti and Aminu Kano.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five features of the 1979 Constitution of Nigeria. [10 marks]
(b) State five differences between the 1963 and the 1979 Constitutions. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Executive presidential system with a President as head of state and government
2 marks: Bicameral National Assembly (Senate and House of Representatives)
2 marks: Federal character principle
2 marks: Federal structure of 19 states with listed powers
2 marks: Entrenched fundamental rights and fundamental objectives and directive principles
1 mark: 1963 parliamentary; 1979 presidential
1 mark: 1963 ceremonial President and Prime Minister; 1979 executive President
1 mark: 1963 fusion of powers; 1979 separation of powers
1 mark: 1963 four regions; 1979 nineteen states
1 mark: Federal character and directive principles only in 1979
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution created an executive presidency, a bicameral National Assembly, nineteen states, the federal character principle and a chapter of fundamental objectives alongside entrenched rights. Unlike the 1963 parliamentary constitution with a ceremonial President, a Prime Minister, fusion of powers and four regions, it embodied separation of powers and a single executive.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem:
(a) Explain five reasons why Nigeria adopted a federal system of government. [10 marks]
(b) State five problems of federalism in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Ethnic, cultural and religious diversity
2 marks: Large size and population of the country
2 marks: Fear of domination of minorities by majority groups
2 marks: Colonial legacy of regionalism (Richards and Lyttelton constitutions)
2 marks: Desire for unity in diversity and economic viability of a large market
1 mark: Revenue allocation disputes
1 mark: Census controversies
1 mark: Agitation for state creation/minority fears
1 mark: Over-concentration of power at the centre
1 mark: Resource control and secessionist agitation
questions.explanation: Federalism suited Nigeria because of its diversity, size and population, minority fears of domination, the colonial pattern of regional development and the wish to unite different peoples while letting them manage local affairs. Problems include revenue allocation, census disputes, demands for new states, a strong centre that weakens states, resource control and separatist agitation.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five principles of Nigeria's foreign policy. [10 marks]
(b) Give five reasons why Africa is regarded as the centrepiece of Nigeria's foreign policy. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of other states
2 marks: Non-interference in the internal affairs of other states
2 marks: Peaceful settlement of disputes
2 marks: Non-alignment
2 marks: Promotion of African unity and eradication of colonialism and racism
1 mark: Nigeria's large population and economy in Africa
1 mark: Commitment to decolonisation of Africa
1 mark: Security of its neighbourhood
1 mark: Promotion of regional economic integration (ECOWAS)
1 mark: Cultural ties with African peoples and the black world
questions.explanation: Nigeria's foreign policy rests on respect for sovereignty, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes, non-alignment and the promotion of African unity and liberation. Africa is the centrepiece because of Nigeria's size and resources, its commitment to ending colonialism and apartheid, its security interest in its neighbours, its leadership of regional integration and its cultural links with Africa and the diaspora.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the six principal organs of the United Nations. [6 marks]
(b) Explain three functions of the Security Council. [6 marks]
(c) State three contributions of Nigeria to the United Nations. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: General Assembly
1 mark: Security Council
1 mark: Economic and Social Council
1 mark: Trusteeship Council
1 mark: International Court of Justice
1 mark: Secretariat
2 marks: Maintains international peace and security
2 marks: Investigates disputes and recommends methods of settlement
2 marks: Imposes sanctions or authorises peacekeeping/military action
1 mark: Contribution of troops to UN peacekeeping missions
1 mark: Payment of dues and service of Nigerians in UN posts
1 mark: Service as non-permanent member of the Security Council/leadership against apartheid
questions.explanation: The UN's principal organs are the General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council, International Court of Justice and Secretariat. The Security Council maintains peace and security, investigates disputes, recommends settlement and may impose sanctions or authorise force. Nigeria has contributed troops to peacekeeping, served several times on the Security Council, provided senior officials and championed the anti-apartheid cause.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five achievements of military regimes in Nigeria between 1966 and 1999. [10 marks]
(b) State five ways in which military rule differed from civilian democratic rule. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Preservation of national unity through the civil war and the 3Rs
2 marks: Creation of states and the 1976 local government reform
2 marks: Establishment of the NYSC (1973) and unity schools
2 marks: Relocation of the capital to Abuja
2 marks: Infrastructure development and transition programmes leading to civilian rule
1 mark: Rule by decrees instead of Acts of a legislature
1 mark: Suspension of the constitution
1 mark: No elected legislature
1 mark: Restriction of rights and freedom of the press
1 mark: Leaders not chosen through elections
questions.explanation: Military regimes kept Nigeria united through the civil war, created states, reformed local government, set up the NYSC and unity schools, moved the capital to Abuja and built infrastructure, while also designing transitions to civil rule. Unlike democratic rule, they governed by decrees, suspended constitutions, abolished elected legislatures, curtailed rights and press freedom and were not chosen by the people.
